**The one kernel caller that could not stay as it was.** `BoundaryDependencyTest`'s rule B found
exactly one violation after the move:

```
Observers/UserObserver.php: App\Modules\Ride\Services\ScoreService
```

`UserObserver` is kernel code (the owner's layout keeps observers and models where they are) and it is
*not* an entrypoint, so it cannot sit in the exemption list; it calls `initializeScore()` on user
creation to lay down the starting trust score. The fix is a port change, and it is the only place in
this batch where a port gained a method that writes:

`App\Modules\Ride\Contracts\ScoreServiceInterface` now also declares
`initializeScore(User $user): UserScore`, with a docblock that says exactly why it is the exception:
it takes no amount, it is safe to call twice, it delegates to the single creation path the ledger
already owns, and it is the one lifecycle write the account-creation observer has to make. The
interface's existing warning against widening it to mutations still stands and is still quoted there,
so the next reader sees the decision rather than an unexplained extra method. `ScoreService` already
implemented `ScoreServiceInterface` and already had that method with that signature, so no behaviour
changed; `UserObserver` now takes the port and resolves to the same singleton.

### 247. Stage 1, phase 3 - the five-order matrix and the leftover-row probe

The five modules are in place, so the last gate is the one that proves the suite does not depend on
which tests ran before it. Five serialised runs of the **full** suite, one after another, on the
scratch database, each followed by the leftover-rows probe:

| Order | Result | Tests | Assertions | Skipped | Leftover rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| default | green (exit 0) | 3046 | 13068 | 2 | clean - 0 in all 30 guarded tables |
| reverse | green (exit 0) | 3046 | 13075 | 2 | clean - 0 in all 30 guarded tables |
| random seed 11 | green (exit 0) | 3046 | 13074 | 2 | clean - 0 in all 30 guarded tables |
| random seed 20261102 | green (exit 0) | 3046 | 13073 | 2 | clean - 0 in all 30 guarded tables |
| random seed 7919 | green (exit 0) | 3046 | 13082 | 2 | clean - 0 in all 30 guarded tables |

Every order: the same 3046 tests, the same 2 skips, no failures, no errors, and no rows left behind in
any of the 30 guarded tables. The snapshot corpus is inside this selection and compares byte-for-byte in
all five orders, so "green in every order" is the proof that the corpus and the fixtures do not depend
on execution order.

One honest note on the numbers: the **assertion** total moves a little between orders (13068 - 13082).
That is expected and not a red flag - some tests assert inside a loop over rows they query, so the
number of assertions depends on how many rows the fixtures produced in that run, and the row set itself
depends on which tests ran before. The invariants that matter - test count, skip count, failure count,
and the leftover-row probe - are identical in all five orders. This is also what makes the batch rule
"the default-order full suite is green" meaningful rather than a coin flip: the default order is not
special, it just happens to be the one recorded per commit.

Runs were serialised deliberately: each one is `php vendor/bin/phpunit --no-coverage` with only the
ordering flag changed, and the probe is a separate PHP process that boots the app, asks the leak
detector for the guarded tables and prints the non-zero ones. `SNAPSHOT_UPDATE` is removed from the
environment by the runner before the first run, so no run could have regenerated the corpus.---

| `ModuleBoundaryTest`, scanned app files | 351 | **353** (floor asserted, so a move cannot make the scan vacuous) |
| `ModuleBoundaryTest`, entrypoint allowlist | 1 file | **12 files** (measured reference counts, shrink-only) |
| `BoundaryDependencyTest` / `CrossContextBoundaryTest` scanned-file floors | none | **340** each |

Two rules were re-pointed rather than relaxed, and both are worth stating plainly because they are
where a move could have hidden a problem:

* Both scanners classified a file by its **first path segment**, so `app/Modules/...` was invisible to
  every layer rule and every context pair - the vacuous pass the owner warned about. Both now derive
  the layer and the context from `Modules/<Name>/<Layer>` and `Modules/<Name>`, with `Contracts/`
  treated as SHARED (a port is the published boundary and must not create an edge), exactly the role
  `app/Interfaces/` played before. Both assert a scanned-file floor.
* Several `assertCeiling`-style Review tests sweep a directory or a file list and only fail when a
  count grows, so losing files makes them pass silently. Three of them were reading the controller tree
  (`RV13ExceptionCodeAsStatusTest`, `ExceptionMessageLeakRatchetTest` twice, `RV33BoundaryDependencyTest`'s
  domain exemption) and now read the module tree too; the rest were re-pointed by path (the inventory
  in section 243.a) and the identical file set they measured before the moves is what they measure now.

### 249. Stage 1.5 item 1 - the dangling import that a path-based move could not see, and two ratchets for the class of bug

**The bug.** `RideServiceProvider` imported `App\Services\Score\ScorePolicyFactory` and registered
`$this->app->singleton(ScorePolicyFactory::class)`. That class does not exist - the score policy factory
is `App\Modules\Ride\Domain\ScorePolicyFactory`. Stage 1 moved the file with `git mv` and rewrote the
imports it found by path; the provider had been *created* in phase 1 by hand, so its `use` line named a
namespace that only existed before the move. The container therefore held a registration for a string
that can never resolve. Nothing failed, because nothing in the suite happens to resolve that binding:
`ScoreLedger` builds the factory itself (RV-11's change), so the broken binding sat there silently.

That is the general hazard of every move in stage 1: the compiler never sees a class name that is only
ever used as a string or in a dead binding, and `git mv` cannot tell a stale reference from a live one.

**The fix.** `use App\Modules\Ride\Domain\ScorePolicyFactory;`, registration unchanged. Verified two
ways: the name resolves through the autoloader, and `ProviderWiringTest` now makes the binding and
asserts it returns an instance of that class.

**The ratchets.** Two new tests in `tests/Feature/AppFuture`:

`DanglingImportTest` scans `app/`, `tests/`, `routes/`, `config/`, `database/` and `scripts/` and
checks every `App\...` token against the autoloader - the same autoloader the container uses.

| Number | Value |
|---|---|
| files scanned | 776 |
| `App\` tokens checked | 2337 |
| dangling tokens before the fix | 11 (1 live import + 10 stale reference comments) |
| dangling tokens after | **0** (baseline) |
| scanned-file floor | 750 |
| token floor | 2000 |

Two rules keep it from crying wolf: a token that is a **declared namespace** in the scanned tree, or a
token that is a **prefix** of one (the character after it is a backslash, `<`, `.` or a backtick) is
prose, not a class name. Without them the scan reports `App\Console\Commands` - the `namespace` line of
every command - as missing. A third test proves the checker can see a bad name at all: it feeds it a
source string with two invented classes and one real one, and requires the two to be reported and the
real one not to be. Without that, "0 dangling" could equally mean "the tokenizer is broken".

`ProviderWiringTest` reads the five module providers plus `app\Support\ContainerBindings.php` and, for
each registration, asserts the names exist, the abstract is bound, it resolves through the container,
it is an instance of the concrete it was bound to, and a `singleton` really is shared:

| Provider | Registrations |
|---|---|
| Communication | 10 |
| Money | 18 |
| Ride | 15 |
| Identity | 18 |
| Console | 15 |
| `ContainerBindings` | 1 |
| **total** | **77** (floor 70) |

This is the test that would have caught the bug in phase 1: it resolves all 77 bindings, including the
one that was broken before this commit. Its own parser is proved by a fixture that mixes a no-concrete
and an abstract/concrete registration.

**What the new ratchet found besides the import** - ten stale reference comments, all re-pointed (they
are references, not history, so leaving them would have meant shipping a name that resolves nowhere):

| File | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `app/DTOs/Score/ScoreSnapshot.php` | `App\Domain\Score\Policies` | `app/Modules/Ride/Domain/Policies` |
| `app/Modules/Money/Services/PassengerWalletCharger.php` | `App\Services\Profile`, `App\Services\Payment` | `app/Modules/Identity/Services`, `app/Modules/Money/Services` |
| `app/Modules/Money/Contracts/PaymentStrategyFactoryInterface.php` | `RIDE -> App\Interfaces -> App\Services\Payment` | `RIDE -> app/Interfaces -> app/Services/Payment` |
| `app/Modules/Money/Contracts/PassengerWalletChargerInterface.php` | `App\Services\Profile`, `App\Services\Payment` | `app/Modules/Identity/Services`, `app/Modules/Money/Services` |
| `app/Modules/Money/Providers/MoneyServiceProvider.php` | `App\Domain\Payment` | `app/Modules/Money/Domain/Strategies` |
| `app/Modules/Console/Providers/ConsoleServiceProvider.php` | `App\Services\Staff` | `app/Modules/Identity/Services` |
| `app/Modules/Identity/Contracts/TokenRevokerInterface.php` | `App\Services` | `app/Services` |
| `tests/Feature/AppFuture/BoundaryDependencyTest.php` | `App\Services` x4 | `app/Services` |
| `tests/Feature/AppFuture/CrossContextBoundaryTest.php` | `App\Services\Wallet`, `App\Interfaces` | `app/Modules/Money/Services`, `app/Interfaces` |
| `config/l5-swagger.php` | a commented-out `// new \App\SwaggerProcessors\SchemaQueryParameter(),` example | deleted (dead vendor template text) |

Note what happened to two of them: writing the *live* module namespace into a comment in a kernel file
(`app/DTOs/Score/ScoreSnapshot.php`) and into the Money module naming Identity's implementation
(`PassengerWalletCharger*`) turned `ModuleBoundaryTest` red - the boundary ratchet reads docblocks too.
Those four items were rewritten as **path** form (`app/Modules/...`), which is what the prose meant
anyway: a historical note about where a file used to live. The two ratchets therefore constrain each
other in a useful way: `DanglingImportTest` forbids a name that resolves nowhere, `ModuleBoundaryTest`
forbids a resolvable name that crosses a boundary, and the honest way to write history is the path.

**Commit.** `Stage 1.5 item 1` - this commit. Files changed: `RideServiceProvider` (the fix), the nine
reference comments above, `config/l5-swagger.php` (one dead comment line), and the two new tests.

**Full default-order suite (the batch's hard rule):** `Tests: 3050, Assertions: 13086, Skipped: 2` -
OK (16:34 of runtime, finished 05:13), on `127.0.0.1:3399/t3_batch`. 3046 + the four new tests (two in `DanglingImportTest`, two in
`ProviderWiringTest`). Snapshot corpus byte-identical (`MANIFEST.json` still 213 files,
`SNAPSHOT_UPDATE=1` never used), leak guard clean inside the run, whole-tree Pint PASS.
Nothing pushed; branch `Agentic` only.---

### 250. Stage 1.5 item 2 - the vacuity sweep: every scanner now proves it read something

A ratchet of the form "no file in this tree does X" passes for two very different reasons: the tree is
clean, or the tree was never read. Stage 1 moved 202 files into modules, which is exactly the change
that turns the second reason into the common one - a sweep still pointed at the old directory finds
nothing and reports success. The owner asked for the full list, a floor on each, and a proof that each
floor is load-bearing.

**Method.** For every test under `tests/` that scans a directory or namespace and asserts a ceiling,
`== 0`, or "no hits", a floor was added at the point where the file list exists: an
`assertGreaterThanOrEqual(N, count(...))` where N is the measured count on 2026-11-03. Then each floor
was proved in a scratch run: the scan root was temporarily replaced with an empty directory, the test
was run, and it had to go red. Every mutation was applied to a copy and restored in the same command; no
commented-out switch, no env flag, nothing left in the tree.

**The full list (23 scanners).**

| # | Test | What it scans | Assertion shape | Floor added | Empty-path run |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `AppFuture/BoundaryDependencyTest` | 353 app files | 9 layer ceilings + baseline | already 340 (stage 1) | **RED** |
| 2 | `AppFuture/CrossContextBoundaryTest` | 353 app files | 20 pair baselines | already 340 (stage 1) | **RED** |
| 3 | `AppFuture/ModuleBoundaryTest` | 353 app files, 5 modules | rules A-E, ceiling 5 | already 353 + per-module | **RED** |
| 4 | `AppFuture/DanglingImportTest` | 776 files, 6 trees | dangling == 0 | already 750 files / 2000 tokens (item 1) | **RED** |
| 5 | `Review/RV13ExceptionCodeAsStatusTest` | 39 controller files | offenders == 0 | **35** | **RED** (both roots; see below) |
| 6 | `Review/ExceptionMessageLeakRatchetTest` | 39 controller files | ceiling + `logged > 0` | **35** | **RED** |

| 11 | `Review/RV30DataModelHygieneTest` | 85 migrations | mismatches == 0 | **80** | **RED** |
| 12 | `Review/RV38LazyArmingMechanismTest` | 26 model files | every model uses the trait | **24** (was only `notEmpty`) | **RED** |

(The table runs to 24 rows because `RV39SeederHygieneTest` has two independent sweeps with separate

**Out of scope, deliberately.** `Review/CiMySqlDriverTest::test_file_exists()` walks `tests/` but it is

**Two findings the sweep itself produced.**

1. **`RV16`'s kernel half was already dead.** Its glob was

### 251. Stage 1.5 item 3 - the entrypoint allowlist names zero production files

**Before.** `ENTRYPOINT_ALLOWLIST` held twelve files: six production entrypoints and six dev-only tools.
The production six were not there because anyone thought implementation names were fine in an
entrypoint; they were there because the surface each one needed was published by no port:

| File | What it reached for | Why no port existed |
|---|---|---|
| `Console/Commands/CleanupExpiredStaffTokens` | `StaffJwtService::cleanupExpiredTokens()` | cleanup was never on `StaffJwtInterface` |
| `Console/Commands/CleanupExpiredTokens` | `JwtService::cleanupExpiredTokens()` | cleanup was never on `TokenRevokerInterface` |
| `Console/Commands/ResolveExpiredNoshowReports` | `Noshowservice::resolveExpiredReports()` | the Ride no-show surface had no port at all |
| `Console/Commands/RotateAdminPasswordCommand` | `StaffJwtService::revokeAllTokens()` | `TokenRevokerInterface` existed but only `JwtService` implemented it |
| `Http/Middleware/StaffJwtMiddleware` | `StaffJwtService::decodeToken()/validateTokenVersion()`, `EmployeeManagementService` | decode-and-rehydrate was deliberately not published (audit sec 244) |
| `Http/Middleware/Support/JwtAuthHandler` | `JwtService::decodeToken()/findUserCached()/validateTokenVersion()`, `BanService::liftExpiredBan()` | same, plus the ban surface had no port |

**After.** Six ports were added in the owning module's `Contracts`, each bound in that module's
provider to the same singleton the concrete already was - no lifetime changed, no constructor of any
service changed, no method signature changed:

| New port (owning module) | Methods | Bound to |
|---|---|---|
| `Identity/Contracts/UserTokenCleanupInterface` | `cleanupExpiredTokens(): int` | `JwtService` (singleton) |
| `Identity/Contracts/StaffTokenCleanupInterface` | `cleanupExpiredTokens(): int` | `StaffJwtService` (singleton) |
| `Identity/Contracts/UserTokenVerifierInterface` | `decodeToken()`, `findUserCached()`, `validateTokenVersion()` | `JwtService` (singleton) |
| `Identity/Contracts/StaffTokenVerifierInterface` | `decodeToken()`, `validateTokenVersion()` | `StaffJwtService` (singleton) |
| `Console/Contracts/BanLifterInterface` | `liftExpiredBan(): bool` | `BanService` |
| `Ride/Contracts/NoShowReportInterface` | `resolveExpiredReports(): int` | `Noshowservice` (singleton) |

`StaffJwtService` also declares `TokenRevokerInterface` now (it already had the matching
`revokeAllTokens(int): void`), so the rotation command depends on the port that already existed rather
than on a new one. `StaffJwtMiddleware` takes `EmployeeManagementInterface` for its second dependency -
the port `EmployeeManagementService` already had.

The user/staff split is deliberate and is the one design judgement in this item: a cleanup or
verification port that covered both would have to be generic over the subject type, and the two token
families (separate secrets, separate tables, separate `ver` claims) are exactly the kind of thing that
must not be blurred behind one interface to make a list shorter.

**Why this is behaviour-preserving.** The middleware and commands receive a different *type name* and
the identical *object*: every binding points at the same singleton the container was already resolving,
and every port method is a pass-through to the method that was being called before. No auth rule, claim
check, ban check, token secret, sweep filter or HTTP response was touched. The six entrypoints' tests
(`tests/Feature/Console`, `tests/Feature/Auth`, `tests/Feature/Staff`, `tests/Unit/Middleware`, the
admin attribution tests) were run before the commit: **469 tests, 1067 assertions, OK**.

**The dev-only six.** The other six entries were not converted, because converting them would mean
publishing the no-show penalty surface, `BookingService` and the chat bridge as ports purely so that
state-fabricating tools could call them - an API decision for a later batch, not a mechanical move (sec
244 parked it). They are now covered by **one** directory-level exemption:

```php
private const ENTRYPOINT_DIRECTORY_EXEMPTIONS = [
    'Console/Testing/' => 'dev-only tools, loaded only when the environment is local or testing',
];
```

The reason is a property of the registration, not of any command: `App\Console\Kernel::commands()`
loads `__DIR__.'/Testing'` only inside `if ($this->app->environment(['local', 'testing']))`, so on a
production box those classes are never registered and nothing - route, command or queue payload - can
reach them. Naming that as one prefix means a seventh dev tool does not need the allowlist edited.

**The new test, and what it does not prove.** `tests/Feature/AppFuture/DevCommandRegistrationTest`
pins the exemption from both sides: the guard must exist, must test exactly `local` and `testing`, must
be the only environment guard in the file, and must be the single load of that directory; and the five
dev commands must actually be registered in the testing environment (a guard that silently stopped
loading the directory would make the exemption pointless rather than safe), with a floor of 8 files
(6 commands + 2 `Support` classes) so the exemption cannot cover an empty directory. It does **not**
boot a second application with `APP_ENV=production`: re-bootstrapping the console kernel inside a test
re-runs `routes/console.php` and re-registers commands, which is a fragile thing to assert with. The
guard's shape is asserted instead, and this limitation is stated here rather than glossed over.

`ModuleBoundaryTest` rule C now reports the measured implementation-naming entrypoints against an empty
list, and asserts the directory exemption covers at least 6 files (non-vacuity, empty-path-proved the
same way as item 2). Its stale class docblock - which still described the phase-1 exemption as "one
artisan command" and the kernel Contracts number as 87 - was corrected in the same commit, since this
item is what made both untrue.

**Commit.** `Stage 1.5 item 3` - this commit. Files changed: **6 new ports**, 4 services gaining
`implements`, 3 providers gaining 6 bindings and 2 imports, the 6 entrypoints, `ModuleBoundaryTest`
(empty allowlist + directory exemption + non-vacuity floor + docblock), and 1 new test file. Ratchet
numbers: `ENTRYPOINT_ALLOWLIST` **12 files -> 0 files**; directory exemptions 0 -> 1 (8 files);
`KERNEL_CONTRACTS_CEILING` unchanged at 5 (the two middleware are entrypoints and were never counted
by rule D).

**Full default-order suite (the batch's hard rule):** `Tests: 3052, Assertions: 13285, Skipped: 2` -
OK, on `127.0.0.1:3399/t3_batch`. Snapshot corpus byte-identical (`MANIFEST.json` still 213 files,
`SNAPSHOT_UPDATE=1` never used), leak guard clean inside the run, whole-tree Pint PASS.
Nothing pushed; branch `Agentic` only.---

### 252. Stage 1.5 item 4 - the module graph as data: one cycle cut, four declared

**The matrix.** Every module-to-module edge that exists today, counted from code only - comments and
docblocks are stripped before matching, because this repository keeps its history in docblocks and a
note about an old namespace must not read as a live edge. Port counts are distinct Contracts names per
pair; implementation edges are **0** everywhere (that is `ModuleBoundaryTest` rule A's job, and
`ModuleGraphTest` asserts it again on this graph).

| from \ to | Communication | Money | Ride | Identity | Console |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Communication** | - | - | - | **0 (was 1)** | 2 |
| **Money** | 1 | - | - | 1 | - |
| **Ride** | 1 | 5 | - | 1 | - |
| **Identity** | 1 | 1 | 2 | - | 1 |
| **Console** | 3 | 3 | 2 | 6 | - |

14 directed edges, 208 module PHP files scanned, ~43 files carrying at least one cross-module
Contracts reference.

**The four cycles, with the specific files and ports.**

| Cycle | This direction | That direction |
|---|---|---|
| Communication <-> Console | `Communication/Http/Controllers/ContactController.php` -> `Console/Contracts/{EmployeeManagementInterface, SupportAgentRoutingInterface}` | 7 Console files -> `Communication/Contracts/NotificationPort`; `StaffChatController` -> `{ChatMessageHandlerInterface, ChatRepositoryInterface}` |
| Communication <-> Identity | `Communication/Providers/CommunicationServiceProvider.php` -> `Identity/Contracts/OtpMailInterface` | `Identity/{PassengerProfileController, Services/VerificationSubmissionService}` -> `Communication/Contracts/NotificationPort` |
| Money <-> Identity | `Money/Http/Controllers/WalletController.php` -> `Identity/Contracts/EmailOtpServiceInterface` | `Identity/Http/Controllers/PassengerProfileController.php` -> `Money/Contracts/PassengerWalletChargerInterface` |
| Ride <-> Identity | `Ride/Services/RideValidationService.php` -> `Identity/Contracts/DocumentVerificationInterface` | `Identity/Http/Controllers/ProfileController.php` -> `Ride/Contracts/{ScoreServiceInterface, UserRideStatsInterface}` |

(The owner's list also named `Communication<->Console`, `Communication<->Identity`, `Money<->Identity`
and `Ride<->Identity`; the fifth pair in the graph, `Console <-> Identity`, was already declared in the
stage 1 map and is listed with the rest.)

**The cut: Communication <-> Identity is gone.** Communication -> Identity was exactly one line in the
whole module tree - the `OtpMailInterface` binding in `CommunicationServiceProvider`, placed there by
stage 1 with the reasoning that mail delivery is Communication's transport (the boundary map puts the
kernel `Mail/` directory in the Communication context). But `OtpMailInterface` is **Identity's** port,
so binding it from Communication meant one module naming another module's Contracts: an edge, and -
since Identity already notifies through Communication's `NotificationPort` - a cycle.

Two homes were tried, and the first one is worth recording because a ratchet caught it:

1. **Identity's own provider.** Move the binding there and Identity names the kernel class
   `App\Mail\OtpMailer` - which rule A of `ModuleBoundaryTest` allows (a module may name the kernel).
   `ModuleGraphTest` then measured Communication -> Identity as 0 and the cycle as gone. But
   `CrossContextBoundaryTest` failed it: in the *context* map the kernel `Mail/` directory belongs to
   the Communication context, so this was a new `IDENTITY_to_COMM` edge against a baseline of 0. The
   fix for that would have been to raise a baseline, which this batch forbids, so the attempt was
   rolled into the next one.
2. **The kernel catalogue** (`App\Support\ContainerBindings`), and this is where it stayed. The
   implementation is a kernel class and the port is a module port; the kernel is explicitly allowed to
   name module Contracts, so the kernel is the natural place to wire a kernel class to one. A new
   `registerKernelPortImplementations()` holds it, `bind()` not `singleton()` (exactly the lifetime it
   had), and neither module provider names the other's Contracts for it. `CrossContextBoundaryTest`
   stays at 0 for `IDENTITY_to_COMM` because the kernel is not a context, `ModuleBoundaryTest` rule D
   does not move because `ContainerBindings` is an entrypoint and names Contracts only, and
   `ModuleGraphTest` measures Communication -> Identity as **0**.

The other four cycles are **declared uncut**, with the reason recorded next to each in
`ModuleGraphTest::UNCUT_CYCLES`:

- **Communication <-> Console** - `ContactController` (`POST /api/contact`) needs to know which support
  agent is least loaded and to have that agent's shadow user, **to build its response**. An event
  cannot return the agent, and a kernel listener would be a sixth kernel file naming module Contracts -
  the ceiling is 5 and it is shrink-only. Rejected alternatives: move the controller into Console
  (hands a passenger-facing endpoint to the back-office module), or move the two port declarations into
  Communication (launders Console's ownership of employees and support routing).
- **Console <-> Identity** - Console authenticates staff through Identity's `EmployeeAuthInterface` and
  `StaffJwtInterface`; Identity reaches back for `EmployeeRepositoryInterface` because batch 233's
  context map puts staff **authentication** in Identity while employee **records** stay in Console.
  Cutting it means moving one of those two things, i.e. contradicting the map.
- **Identity <-> Money** - an OTP-verified withdrawal (Money -> Identity) versus a wallet top-up
  (Identity -> Money). Both need a return value, so no event can carry them; cutting either means
  moving an HTTP endpoint between modules, which is endpoint ownership, not a port move.
- **Identity <-> Ride** - driver-document verification (Ride -> Identity) versus ride stats and score
  on the profile page (Identity -> Ride). Same shape as Identity <-> Money.

**The ratchet.** `tests/Feature/AppFuture/ModuleGraphTest.php` (3 tests) pins the whole thing:

1. the measured directed edge set **and its per-edge port counts** must equal the declared table
   (shrink-only), with floors on scanned files (>= 200), edges (>= 14) and cross-module files (>= 30);

  16 longer loops are listed as derived data, and every longer loop must contain a declared mutual pair
   as adjacent modules - so a loop that is a *new* design decision rather than a consequence of the
   declared pairs fails the test with its own name in the message.

### 253. Stage 1.5 item 5 - assertion-count determinism: two tests, two different causes

The method was the owner's: run the whole suite twice with JUnit logs, once in default order and once
with `--order-by=reverse`, then diff **per-test** assertion counts. Totals are useless here - they hide
the case where one test gains what another loses, which is exactly what one of the two causes turned out
to be.

**The diff.** 3055 tests in both orders; 13183 vs 13178 assertions. `phpunit --log-junit` gives every
test case an `assertions` attribute, so the comparison is exact. It found exactly two files:

1. **`Feature/Payment/LedgerRandomizedPropertyTest` - 220 data sets renamed per run.** Its data provider
   is seeded, but the default seed was `random_int(1, 999_999_999)` - deliberately, to keep the property
   test from becoming a fixture. Consequence: every run had different case labels
   (`charge-price-6933.98-seats-1-004` on one run, something else on the next), so *every* case looked
   like a test that only existed in one log; and because a scenario carrying a second booking asserts one
   more time, three cases reported 13 assertions on one run and 12 on the next.
2. **`Feature/AppFuture/CrossContextBoundaryTest` - the memoised scan asserted.** `scan()` is cached in a
   static for the twenty pair baselines, and it contained the scanner's non-vacuity floor
   (`appFiles() >= 340`). PHPUnit attributes an assertion to the test that executes it, so the data set
   that happened to run first paid the floor and the others did not:
   `RIDE_to_MONEY` 6 -> 4 and `CONSOLE_to_COMM` 4 -> 6, with the **total unchanged at 82**. A totals-only
   comparison would have called this deterministic.

**The fixes, both of the kind the owner named.**

- *Fix the data source* (case 1). `LedgerPropertySeed::DEFAULT_SEED = 20261103`, and the selection is now
  three-way: `LEDGER_SEED=<int>` replays a seed exactly, `LEDGER_SEED=random` explores a fresh scenario
  set per run, unset uses the default. The docblocks in both files say why the default flipped: a random
  default is incompatible with an assertion count that is checked across orders, and exploration is one
  environment variable away.
- *Make the loop explicit* (case 2). No assertions inside the memoised `scan()` any more. The scan-level
  floors moved into a dedicated non-provider test,
  `test_the_scan_walks_the_whole_tree_and_indexes_its_classes()`, which asserts the same three things
  once: `appFiles() >= 340`, the class index `>= 300` entries, and every declared context owning at least
  one file (so a whole row of baselines cannot be vacuous). That is *stronger* than what was there - the
  per-context check is new - and it costs one deterministic set of assertions instead of a set whose owner
  depended on order.

**Evidence.**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| default vs reverse, the two files (245 tests) | **0 per-test differences**, 2645 = 2645 assertions |
| `LedgerRandomizedPropertyTest` twice with the fixed default (224 tests) | **0 per-test differences**, 2551 = 2551 |
| `LEDGER_SEED=random` still works (224 tests) | OK, 2545 assertions - different by design, printed seed |
| full-suite default vs reverse, before the fix | 13183 vs 13178, 5 differing cases in 2 files |
| full-suite default vs reverse, after the fix | see item 8's five-order matrix: all five orders identical |

The full-suite diff found only these two - nothing else in 3055 tests varies with order. That is worth
stating explicitly: the sweep was not limited to the two files it happened to find.

**Commit.** `Stage 1.5 item 5` - this commit. Files changed: 3 test/support files
(`tests/Support/LedgerPropertySeed.php`, `tests/Feature/Payment/LedgerRandomizedPropertyTest.php`,
`tests/Feature/AppFuture/CrossContextBoundaryTest.php`), no application code, no assertion weakened (one
moved and one new check added). Test totals: 3055 -> **3056** (the new scan-floor test).

**Full default-order suite (the batch's hard rule):** `Tests: 3056, Assertions: 13196, Skipped: 2` - OK (21:05 of runtime),
on `127.0.0.1:3399/t3_batch`. Snapshot corpus byte-identical (`MANIFEST.json` still 213 files,

### 255. Stage 1.5 item 7 - the documentation: one architecture map, five module READMEs, five ADRs

Documentation-only commit. No PHP file, no test, no config changed - the whole diff is markdown, which

**`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`** (17 KB) is the map, and it is written so that a reader can find the rule that
will stop them rather than only the shape they are looking at:

1. the shape (five modules, a kernel, one deployable) and why not services;
2. the kernel: what is in it, why each directory is shared, the five-file Contracts ceiling, and the
   `FileUploadService` decision with its rejected alternatives;
3. the modules table: files, ports, what each depends on and who depends on it;
4. the **module graph** - the 14-edge matrix, the four declared cycles with their reasons, the cut that
   removed `Communication -> Identity`, and the failed first attempt that `CrossContextBoundaryTest`
   caught;
5. ports: the rule, and the five-step checklist for adding one, each step naming the ratchet that will
   complain if it is skipped;
6. the ratchets table: every rule, its baseline or ceiling, and the two properties that make them
   trustworthy (they count what they scanned; they cross-check each other);
7. entrypoints: the allowlist at zero and the one directory exemption;
8. "where does a new class go" - the decision tree a developer actually needs;
9. "how this document can rot" - the numbers are measurements and the ratchets are the truth.

**Five module READMEs** (`app/Modules/<M>/README.md`), one per module, each with the same five sections:
what it owns (by directory and by service), its public Contracts table (port, implementation, consumers
today), who may call it and what it may call, what it may not do, and where its tests are. They are
deliberately concrete: the Console README names the two declared cycles it is half of, the Ride README
names the no-show surface that was deliberately *not* published as a broad port, the Identity README
explains why the token ports are split user/staff rather than merged.

**Five ADRs** (`docs/adr/`, plus an index):

| ADR | Decision | The alternatives it rejects |
|---|---|---|
| 0001 | modular monolith, not microservices | microservices (escrow + ledger transactionality), plain folders, a package per module |
| 0002 | boundaries enforced by ratchets | PHPStan/deptrac architecture rules, code review, composer boundaries |
| 0003 | ports live in each module's `Contracts` | the flat `app/Interfaces`, ports in the consumer's module, "just be careful" |
| 0004 | jobs, listeners, notifications stay in the kernel | moving them (queue payloads store class names), delegating from the job, stable payload aliases |
| 0005 | `app/Console/Testing` is exempt as a directory | per-file entries, moving the tools into `tests/`, gating each command on `isProduction()` |

Each ADR states the context, the decision, the consequences (including the ones that cost something -
one transaction spanning three modules, a kernel that keeps an admittedly unclean surface, a random
property test that had to lose its random default), and the rejected alternatives with the reason.

### 257. Stage 2 Phase A (A1) - a failed INSERT stops writing its bound values to the log

**The finding, and the shape of it.** Laravel builds a `QueryException` message as the driver's text
*plus* the connection, the full statement and every bound value:

```
SQLSTATE[42S22]: Column not found: 1054 Unknown column 'x' in 'field list'
(Connection: mysql, SQL: insert into `users` (`first_name`, `email`, `password`, `address`)
 values (LeakProbeFirst, leak.probe@example.test, $2y$10$LeakProbeHash..., LeakProbeAddress))
```

So a single `Log::error('Registration failed (Path B)', ['error' => $e->getMessage()])` writes the bcrypt
hash, the name, the email and the address into `storage/logs/laravel.log` - the owner's test log showed
exactly that, for signup and for ride creation (phone, addresses, notes). The same pattern existed
wherever a catch block wraps anything that can reach the database, and in a Laravel application that is
almost everywhere: an INSERT, an UPDATE, `DB::transaction`, an Eloquent `->save()`.

**The sweep.** `app/` has 153 `Log::error` / `Log::warning` / `Log::critical` sites; **126 of them logged
`->getMessage()`**. All 126 now go through one formatter, `App\Support\Logging\SafeExceptionLog::message()`
(new, `app/Support/Logging/`, 46 files changed):

- a `QueryException` becomes `SQLSTATE[<state>]: <driver message>` - the SQLSTATE from `errorInfo[0]`, the
  driver's own text from `errorInfo[2]` (falling back to `getPrevious()->getMessage()`), and nothing else:
  no statement, no bindings, no `(Connection: ..., SQL: ...)` suffix;
- **anything else is returned unchanged**, which is what makes the sweep mechanical rather than 126
  judgement calls about whether a given catch can see a QueryException. A `ValidationException` still logs
  the text it logged before, byte for byte;
- the existing context keys are untouched, so every log line still says what it said plus the safe error
  text. No response body, status code, query or auth rule is affected - nothing here reads or writes
  anything but the log.

Three call sites used `"{$e->getMessage()}"` interpolation (`ProfileController::fetchProfile`,
`EmailOtpService::sendOtp/verifyOtp`) and were rewritten as concatenation: a function call is not valid in
simple interpolation, and the mechanical pass would otherwise have left a literal `{SafeExceptionLog::...}`
in the message.

**The characterization test** (`tests/Feature/Review/Stage2A1LogRedactionTest.php`, 2 tests, 44
assertions) does both halves, because a test that only mocks the exception proves nothing about the real
one:

1. it **causes real MySQL failures** - an INSERT naming a column that does not exist, with the marker
   values as genuine bindings - and asserts the caught `QueryException`'s message really does contain each
   marker (the positive control: without it, "the log is clean" could just mean "the fixture carried
   nothing");
2. it feeds those same two real exceptions through the two production paths that used to log them. Signup
   Path B runs with a repository that throws the real exception; ride creation runs the **real**
   `RideLifecycleHandler` and the real `RideService` (`RideService` is final, so it cannot be mocked - the
   throw happens inside the production call stack from a `DB::listen` callback armed after the request is
   built), and the test asserts the captured log record contains none of the bound values, still carries
   the SQLSTATE, no longer carries `SQL: insert`, and still carries the driver's own words (the offending
   column name) so the line remains useful.

The signup email is asserted separately and deliberately: `'email' => $request->email` is an existing
context key of that log line and A1 keeps the existing keys. The hash, the name and the address arrived
only through the exception message - those are the leak, and they are gone.

**Parked (out of A1's stated scope, one question each, recorded in STATE.md).**

1. `TextMeBotOtpService` line 112 and `WhatsAppOtpService` line 117 log the raw phone number in the
   message (`"Failed to send OTP to $validatedPhone"`), and `WhatsAppOtpService` line 271 logs the whole
   CallMeBot response body. Neither is an exception message, so A1 as specified does not cover them - but
   the second can carry the OTP itself. **Question:** should A2 mask the phone number and the provider
   response body, and is that in scope for log hygiene?
2. `SignupRegistrationHandler` itself keeps `'email' => $request->email` (kept, per "plus the existing
   context keys"). **Question:** should the lookup email move to a hash, or is a single email address in
   the log accepted?

**No existing assertion pinned the old text.** Checked with `git grep` for the four named messages
(`Registration failed (Path B)`, `Ride creation failed`, `resend OTP failed`, `Signup: DB lookup failed`)
across `tests/`: zero hits, so nothing had to be parked for a pinned assertion.

**One ratchet guard had to be re-scoped, and it is not a pinned log text.** The first default-order suite
came back with exactly one failure:

```
Tests\Feature\Review\ExceptionMessageLeakRatchetTest::server_side_logging_of_exception_messages_is_not_counted
Failed asserting that 0 is greater than 0.
```

That guard counts `Log::(error|warning)\([^;]*getMessage\(\)` in the controllers and required the count to be
**greater than zero**, on the reasoning that zero means the scan has gone blind - its own message says "if
this is ever zero, the ratchet is over-broad and should be re-scoped before it blocks legitimate logging".
A1 drove that count to zero on purpose, so the guard as written demanded a live leak: the one thing the
phase removes. It is re-scoped rather than deleted or parked, and the re-scope strengthens it:

- the matcher is proven on a sample string (it still recognises `Log::error('x', ['error' =>
  $e->getMessage()]);`), so the "aimed at the right thing" property is still proven;
- the live count is now asserted to be **exactly 0**, with a message telling the next author to use
  `SafeExceptionLog::message($e)`.

Two other assertions in that same file (`no_controller_may_add_a_new_raw_exception_message_leak`,
`no_controller_returns_a_raw_exception_message_to_a_client`) are untouched and still green: they scan for
exception messages in **client responses**, which A1 never touched. The file's own `MIN_SCANNED_FILES`
floor (stage 1.5 item 2) is untouched, so the scan still proves it walked the controller tree.

**Full default-order suite (the batch's hard rule), first run with `--log-junit` as the owner asked.**
`Tests: 3058, Assertions: 13243, Skipped: 2` - OK. **Wall clock 34:22** (summed test time 34:18), against
the owner's 31:48 and the ~17 min norm. Snapshots byte-identical, leak guard clean inside the run,
whole-tree Pint PASS (791 files).

| # | s | assertions | test |

| 1 | 18.719 | 1 | `Tests\Unit\Broadcasting\NotificationChannelTest::test_channel_class_exists` |
| 2 | 6.418 | 5 | `RV39SeederHygieneTest::test_wallet_phone_numberspaces_do_not_collide_between_the_two_seeders` |

### 258. Stage 2 Phase B1 - the ride fixture writes production-shaped coordinate columns

**The finding.** `rides` carries the geometry columns *and* `pickup_lat` / `pickup_lng` /
`destination_lat` / `destination_lng` (added by `2025_05_22_224859_add_pickup_lat_lng_to_rides_table`,
backfilled from the geometry by `2026_10_05_000001_backfill_ride_lat_lng_from_geometry`).
`Ride::getPickupLocationAttribute()` reads the scalars first and, when they are null, falls back to a
**per-row** `SELECT ST_AsText(pickup_location) AS wkt FROM rides WHERE id = ?` (the RV-24 fast path).

`tests/Support/RideBuilder.php` - the single place that inserts a ride for tests (RV-34) - wrote the
geometry only. Every fixture row therefore had null scalars, every ride response paid one query per ride,
and four committed response snapshots recorded `"pickup_lat": null` / `"pickup_lng": null`: a shape
production never returns.

**The fix.** `RideBuilder::create()` now also writes the four scalar columns (the fixture's own
coordinates: pickup 33.5138 / 36.2765, destination 36.2021 / 37.1343). They are written with `??=`, so a
caller that passes its own via `withAttributes()` still wins, and the geometry insert is untouched: the
axis-order question belongs to RV-25 and this fixture must not silently normalise it.

One test genuinely needs the old row shape: `RV24RideCoordinateReadTest` pins that, with null scalars, the
accessor equals a geometry parse. It gets an explicit opt-in rather than an edited assertion -
`RideBuilder::for()->withoutScalarCoordinates()` - so the assertion text is unchanged and the fallback path
is still covered on purpose.

**The four regenerated response snapshots** (measured: the failing set was exactly these four, no more and
no fewer):

| snapshot | what changed |
|---|---|
| `api/rides/index.json` | `pickup_lat`/`pickup_lng`/`destination_lat`/`destination_lng`: null → `33.51380000` / `36.27650000` / `36.20210000` / `37.13430000` |
| `api/rides/search-get.json` | same four columns, same values |
| `api/rides/search-post.json` | same four columns, same values |
| `api/rides/cancel.json` | same four columns, same values |

Nothing else in those files moved: `git diff` shows only those lines, and no state snapshot changed (the
state corpus does not project the scalar columns - verified before the change: zero state files mention
`pickup_lat`).

**Budgets, re-recorded DOWN** (`tests/Snapshots/query-budgets.json`; the store's `record()` is shrink-only
even under `SNAPSHOT_UPDATE=1`, so no entry could rise):

**40 queries removed** from the snapshot corpus, all of them the per-row geometry fallback. This is the

### 259. Stage 2 Phase B2 (first slice) - a ledger leg can name the row that recorded its own movement

**The finding.** `ledger_entries.wallet_transaction_id` existed, was indexed, was read by
`LedgerService::imbalanceFor()`, and was **null in every row the application ever wrote**: 601 legs across
the 40 state snapshots, zero links. `postTransfer()` accepted one `?WalletTransaction $transaction` and
applied it to every leg, so a two-leg transfer could only ever name one side - and
`postExternalTransfer()` did not accept one at all. The ledger could prove a movement balanced, but not
which single-sided row explained which leg.

**The change (first slice).**

1. `LedgerService::postTransfer()` now accepts a per-leg `wallet_transaction_id`, falling back to the
   call-level transaction when a leg omits it. Backwards compatible in both directions: no leg key means
   exactly the previous behaviour, and the parameter is still optional. That is what makes the remaining
   money paths a mechanical edit each, rather than one large rewrite.
2. `LedgerServiceInterface::postExternalTransfer()` takes `externalTransaction:` and `targetTransaction:`
   instead of one `transaction:`, because the two legs are two different wallets and one row cannot
   describe both. Both are optional and nullable, so a caller that has only one side still works.
3. The three external-capital paths now pass what they already had:
   - `AdminWalletCharger` (admin credit): both sides (it already received the target row as `$transaction`
     and discarded the external row it created);
   - `AdminWalletRequestController` (wallet-request approve): both sides - `recordWalletMovement()` now
     returns the row it writes instead of dropping it, and `settleExternalCapital()` receives it;
   - `PassengerWalletCharger` (passenger charge): the external row only (the target row is written by its
     caller, so it is threaded in the next slice - see the parked item below).

**The Console/module-boundary detail, worth recording.** `AdminWalletRequestController` cannot import
`App\Models\WalletTransaction`: `BoundaryDependencyTest` rule `controllers_to_models` is a **0 baseline** and
it caught the first attempt - including a docblock that merely *mentioned* the FQCN, because the rule scans
tokens. The parameter is therefore untyped, with a comment saying why; the value only travels from the
Console service straight back into the Money port, which owns the type.

**Measured result.** 126 legs now carry a link, 477 remain null (from 0 / 601). The links that appeared are
the external-capital debit legs - and because the snapshot corpus's shared seed funds every wallet through
`injectExternalCapital()`, that one change shows up in **all 40** state files: 40 regenerated, 0 response
snapshots touched, 0 query budgets changed.

**Regeneration (authorised by the phase).** `SNAPSHOT_UPDATE=1 php vendor/bin/phpunit tests/Feature/Snapshots`
rewrote exactly those 40 state files plus `MANIFEST.json` (refreshed with
`php scripts/refresh-snapshot-manifest.php` - this is the B3 step the owner wanted in the same commit). No
other snapshot file changed, which is also evidence the corpus writer is deterministic: a file whose rows did
not change came back byte-identical.

**Verification.** `tests/Feature/Snapshots`, `tests/Feature/Admin`, `tests/Feature/Wallet`,
`tests/Feature/Payment`, `tests/Unit/Services/Admin`, `tests/Unit/Services/Payment`, `tests/Feature/Review`,
`tests/Feature/AppFuture`: **OK, 1515 tests, 8339 assertions, 2 skipped**. One earlier run of the same
selection was red with 41 failures - 40 state snapshots plus the `controllers_to_models` boundary rule - and
both causes are the intended change and the fix recorded above.

**Parked, with the reason (this is the remaining half of B2, not a decision for the owner).** The
Money-internal paths still post legs without a link, because each needs the transactions threaded through
its own private helpers rather than being available at the call site:
`BookingCharge::postChargeLegs` (booking charge - the reference path, two rows already exist),
`CancellationLedgerWriter` (3 sites: driver cancellation, staff cancellation fan-out, time-based
cancellation), `NoShowSettlement` (2 sites), `RidePayout` (2 sites: payout, completion), `CashRideCreationFeeCharger`,
`CashRideDebtClearanceService`, `CashRideFeeRefundService`, and the target side of
`PassengerWalletCharger::injectExternalCapital`. The randomized-property extension
("every new leg links to a transaction of the same wallet and amount") is parked **with** them, because it
cannot pass honestly until they are done: 477 legs would fail it today. Doing it in that order keeps the
property meaningful instead of normalising a half-linked ledger. Next step is recorded in STATE.md.

**One unverified observation, parked rather than fixed.** `PassengerProfileController::chargeWallet()` calls
`recordAdminChargeTransaction()` and then `injectExternalCapital()`, and `recordAdminChargeTransaction()`
*calls `injectExternalCapital()` itself* (line 375). If both run for one charge, the external account is
debited and the inbound legs posted twice for a single passenger credit. I did **not** confirm the money
effect from the state snapshots (the pairs there are consistent with one posting per movement), so this is a
suspicion with a code path, not a finding. **Question:** is the inner call intended (and the outer one
dead), or is this a double-posting bug that should be its own money task before the ledger properties are
tightened?

three errors: `recordDriverCompensation(): Return value must be of type ?App\Models\WalletTransaction, none
returned`. Reaching the end of a function that declares a return type is a `TypeError` - it is *not* an
implicit `null`, even for a nullable type. The fix is the explicit `return null;` after the `if`. Every other
row-writer in this slice returns on all paths, so this was the only instance; it is recorded because the
symptom (a 500 on partial-seat cancellation, logged as `Partial seat cancellation failed`) looks like a
cancellation bug rather than a missing return.

### 264. Stage 2 Phase B2 (sixth slice) - the cash-fee paths link, and a measured double injection in the admin charge

**The change.** `CashRideCreationFeeCharger` (immediate branch), `CashRideDebtClearanceService` and
`CashRideFeeRefundService` now link their legs: each row-writer returns its `WalletTransaction` (or a
wallet-id-keyed map where it writes two), and `postFeeTransfer`, `postDebitClearLegs`, `postRefundLegs` take
optional per-leg transactions. `CashRideCreationFeeCharger::chargeDeferredFee` and
`CashRideFeeRefundService::cancelDeferredDebt`/`recordNoRefund` write zero-amount audit rows and post **no**
legs at all, so there is nothing to link there - the deferred fee becomes a real movement later, and
`CashRideDebtClearanceService::postDebitClearLegs` (the collection of that debt) is linked instead.

`PassengerWalletCharger::injectExternalCapital()` gained an untyped `$targetTransaction = null` (interface
updated too) so the inbound leg can name the receiving wallet's row. The token is untyped on purpose: the
caller is an Identity controller and `BoundaryDependencyTest` rule `controllers_to_models` is a 0 baseline.
Existing three-argument callers - including `tests/Feature/Snapshots/ApiSnapshotTestCase.php:412` - keep
working.

**FINDING (measured, money - PARKED, not fixed).** The admin charge double-injects into External Capital.
`PassengerProfileController::chargeWallet()` calls `$this->recordAdminChargeTransaction(...)` (line 310),
which **itself** calls `injectExternalCapital()` (line 375), and then calls `injectExternalCapital()` again
directly (line 316). The state snapshot for the route proves the money effect - the last 5000 charge of
`admin/passenger-charge-wallet.json`:

| row | amount | previous -> new |
|---|---|---|
| `admin_charge` | +5000 | 1062500 -> 1067500 |
| `external_inbound` | -5000 | -67500 -> -72500 |
| `external_inbound` | -5000 | -72500 -> -77500 |

One `admin_charge` credit, **two** External Capital debits. So for every admin charge the External Capital
wallet loses twice the amount while the passenger gains it once, and the ledger carries two
external->wallet transfers for one movement. Both rows have `posting_key = null`, so nothing rejects the
second. This is a balance/ledger defect, not a display issue - but it changes money semantics, so per the
standing rule it is parked rather than fixed. **Question:** is the inner call (line 375) the intended one and
the outer (line 316) vestigial, or should the pair be collapsed into one injection? Note the second leg's
`transaction_id` is `EXT-ADM-{user}-{uuid}`, so the two rows are distinct rather than colliding.

**Why this also parks the randomized property.** The planned invariant ("every ledger leg written during a
movement links to a transaction of the same wallet and amount") would now *fail* on exactly this case: the
duplicate transfer's target leg has no row to link to. So the property cannot be landed green until both
(a) the remaining unlinked paths are linked - 121 legs still null - and (b) this double injection is
resolved. The two parked items are therefore one dependency, not two.

**Consequence for the freeze, worth flagging now.** This slice links the *inner* injection's target leg, so
the corpus now records the duplicate as expected state (`admin/passenger-charge-wallet.json`). A future fix
to the double injection will change that file, and after B3 the freeze rule forbids `SNAPSHOT_UPDATE=1`. That
fix will therefore need one explicit snapshot-regeneration exception. The code comment at the link site says
so, so it is not lost.

**Measured.** Corpus 481 -> **482 linked** (121 null); one state file regenerated plus `MANIFEST.json`. Only
the passenger-profile charge route exercises these paths, which is why the corpus moves by one even though
every cash-fee leg now links.

**Verification.** `Payment` + `Admin` + `Wallet` + `Bookings` + `Rides` + `AppFuture`: **OK, 594 tests, 3734
assertions**. Then `Snapshots` + `Payment` + `AppFuture`: **OK, 517 tests, 5238 assertions**. `php -l` clean
on all six files; Pint PASS on `app/Modules/Money` (36 files) and the controller.

### 265. Stage 2 Phase B2 (seventh slice) - the seed links too, and the corpus now has exactly one unlinked leg

**The change.** `ApiSnapshotTestCase` seeds three admin charges: it creates the `wallet_transactions` row and
then calls `injectExternalCapital()` without telling it which row recorded the receiving wallet's movement.
The seed now keeps that row and passes it, so the seed's inbound legs name their own side like every
production path does.

**A trap worth recording.** The first attempt wrapped the call as
`$row = $this->stampRow(WalletTransaction::create([...]), ...)`, and `stampRow(Model $row, Carbon $at): void`
returns **void**. So `$row` was `null`, the injection silently behaved exactly as before, and the only
symptom was *the check I was watching*: `SNAPSHOT_UPDATE=1` changed **zero** files and the corpus count did not
move. Without that observation this would have looked like a successful change. The fix is to capture the row
from `WalletTransaction::create()` and stamp it separately.

**Measured, and this is the number that closes B2's linkage work.** Corpus went from 482 linked / 121 null to
**602 linked / 1 null** - 40 state files plus `MANIFEST.json`. Of 603 legs in the corpus, exactly one is
unlinked, and it is the `+5000` leg on wallet 6 in `admin/passenger-charge-wallet.json`: the target leg of the
**duplicate injection** measured in sec 264. So B2's linkage is complete for every leg whose movement has a
row to name; the single exception is not a missing call, it is a money defect. That also sharpens the parked
dependency: the randomized property would now fail on exactly **one** leg, and that leg disappears only when
the double injection is fixed.

**Measured reach.** 40 state files changed, which is what a seed-level change should do - the seed funds every
case's world, so linking it legitimately touches every state snapshot whose ledger contains a seeded charge.
No response snapshot and no query budget moved.

**Verification.** `Snapshots` + `Payment` + `AppFuture`: **OK, 517 tests, 5238 assertions**. `php -l` clean on
the test case.

**B2 status.** Every money path in the objective's list now links: booking charge, payout (both flows),
cancellation refund (driver, staff, time-based), no-show settlement (both), cash creation fee, cash debt
clearance, cash fee refund, wallet-request approve, admin charge, staff cancellation. One leg remains null,
because of a parked defect rather than a missing link.

### 266. Stage 2 Phase B4 - five contract questions, parked with one question each

Nothing here was changed: each item alters a status code, a response shape or an auth rule, which the phase
rules park. Each is recorded with the code I verified and exactly one question so the owner can decide.

**1. 403 vs 404 vs 422 semantics.** Across `app/**/Http/Controllers` the three appear 13 / 51 / 77 times. A
missing resource is a 404 (`findOrFail`), validation is a 422, and "exists but belongs to someone else" is
**sometimes 403 and sometimes 404**, with no single rule saying which. The choice is a real one: 404 hides
whether the row exists (no enumeration), 403 tells the owner honestly. **Question: for a resource that exists
but belongs to another user, should the API answer 403 (explicit) or 404 (hide existence)?** Changing either
way alters status codes on existing endpoints.

**2. The errors envelope.** Two shapes coexist: `{status: 'error', message: ...}` (129 sites, plus 177
`message` keys) and a bare `{error: ...}` (6 sites). A client cannot have one parser. **Question: adopt
`{status, message}` as the single error envelope and convert the six `{error}` endpoints, or keep `{error}`
deliberately for those six?** Either answer changes a public response shape.

**3. `POST /api/profile` and documents.** `ProfileController` returns a computed `documents` array on read
(line 448), but the POST endpoint does not accept or replace documents - uploads go through the document
upload handler (`DocumentUploadHandler:101` stores to `documents` on the public disk). So `documents` is
read-only on the profile payload, which is not stated anywhere a client would look. **Question: is `documents`
deliberately read-only on `POST /api/profile` (documents change only through the upload endpoint), or should
POST accept and replace them?** Accepting them would widen the contract and duplicate the upload rules.

**4. `recent_activities[].date` type.** `AdminReportService::getRecentActivities()` (line 218) builds each
activity array and emits `date` as a formatted string, unlike the ISO-8601 timestamps used elsewhere in the
API. **Question: should `date` be ISO-8601 like the rest of the API, or stay human-formatted for the admin
panel?** Changing it changes a documented-looking field on an admin response.

**5. Self-chat answers 500 instead of 422.** `ChatController` validates
`'user_id' => '...|different:'.$request->user()->id` (line 68). `different:` compares against **another input
field**, not a literal value, so with no input named after the id the rule can never fire; the request then
reaches the insert, the duplicate `(conversation_id, user_id)` row violates the unique index, and the endpoint
answers **500**. `ChatTest::test_cannot_start_conversation_with_self` (line 34) documents this in its own
comment - "either 422 (validation) or 500 (exception) - both mean failure" - so a fix would not break it.
**Question: replace the rule with `not_in:`/an explicit equality check so the endpoint answers 422?** It is a
one-line fix but it changes a status code from 500 to 422, so it is parked rather than slipped into a
refactoring commit.
---

### 267. Stage 2 Phase C1 reconnaissance - the User reverse relations are a hard prerequisite, not a detail

No code was moved in this section. It records what the first module move actually requires, because the
answer changes the order of work.

**Measured blast radius for the Communication module** (the first in the required order), counting explicit
`App\Models\X` references: Conversation 3 app / 1 test, ConversationParticipant 0 / 1, Message 5 / 2,
Notification 2 / 3, UserNotification 2 / 3, PushNotificationToken 1 / 1. Small enough to look mechanical.

**The blocker.** `app/Models/User.php` holds the reverse relations that C2 requires *removed*:

- line 174 `belongsToMany(Conversation::class, 'conversation_participants')`
- line 181 `hasMany(Message::class, 'sender_id')` (sentMessages)
- line 186 `belongsToMany(Notification::class, 'user_notifications')`
- line 193 `hasMany(UserNotification::class)`
- line 198 `hasMany(PushNotificationToken::class)`

These are unqualified references that resolve inside `App\Models`, so the moment those five models leave that
namespace, `User` either needs five cross-module imports - exactly what C2 forbids and what the ownership test
will flag - or the relations must be gone first. So moving Communication is not a file move with a use-line
sweep: it is a relation removal with call-site migration, i.e. C2 work, arriving before the C1 commit that the
plan assumed would come first.

**Also noted while reading:** none of the six models declares `protected $table`, and all six currently rely on
Eloquent's convention. Moving them to a namespaced directory changes the table Eloquent infers
(`app/Modules/Communication/Models/Conversation` would still guess `conversations`, so behaviour would hold by
luck), but the phase rule requires an **explicit** `protected $table` on every moved model - so each of the
six gains one, with the value it resolves to today: `conversations`, `conversation_participants`, `messages`,
`notifications`, `user_notifications`, `push_notification_tokens`.

**Consequence for sequencing.** The defensible order is: build `ModelOwnershipTest` first with a shrink-only
baseline that records today's violations (C2's instrument), remove the `User` reverse relations one module at
a time with their call sites migrated to Readers, and move a module's models in the same commit as its
relations disappear - so the tree never contains a cross-module relation that the new test would reject.
Parked for the owner only if a call site cannot be expressed as a Reader: none found yet, but the call sites
have not been enumerated, which is the next measurement.
---

### 268. Stage 2 Phase C1 - the reverse-relation call sites, counted (and the order it settles)

Following sec 267's open question, every call site of the eight `User` reverse relations was counted
(`->name` occurrences in `app/` and `tests/`):

| relation | app | tests | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `conversations` | 0 | 0 | dead - removable with no call-site work |
| `sentMessages` | 0 | 0 | dead - removable with no call-site work |
| `notifications` | 3 | 0 | small |
| `userNotifications` | 2 | 1 | small |
| `pushTokens` | 1 | 0 | trivial |
| `rides` | 2 | 2 | small (Ride module) |
| `bookings` | 16 | 0 | medium (Ride module) |
| `wallet` | 33 | 88 | heavy (Money module) |

**What this settles.** The Communication relations - the ones that made sec 267 doubt the required order -
total **six call sites**, two of the five relations are entirely unused, and none sit in tests beyond one. So
Communication remains the correct first module, exactly as the phase specifies; the coupling is real but
small. The genuinely expensive work is concentrated in Money (`wallet`, 121 sites) and Ride (`bookings` 16,
`rides` 4), which are modules 2 and 3 in the required order - so difficulty rises in the order the phase
already chose, and the last two modules (Identity, Console) will start from a mostly-clean tree.

**Consequence for how C1 lands.** `App\Models\User` must keep its five Communication relations until C2
replaces them, so the Communication move needs five cross-module imports in `User` as *recorded, shrinking*
debt. That is what the shrink-only baseline is for: the ownership test is built first with today's violations
recorded, the Communication move adds nothing beyond those five, and C2's shrink pass removes them with the
six call sites migrated to a Communication Reader. Starting the reverse-relation removal *before* the model
move would mean writing a Reader for a module whose models have not moved yet - i.e. doing the work twice.

### 269. Stage 2 Phase C1, module 1 of 5: Communication moved, and what moving it actually cost

**Moved** (`git mv`, so history follows): six models into `app/Modules/Communication/Models` - Conversation,
ConversationParticipant, Message, Notification, UserNotification, PushNotificationToken - each with an
**explicit** `protected $table` stating the name it previously inferred by convention (`conversations`,
`conversation_participants`, `messages`, `notifications`, `user_notifications`,
`push_notification_tokens`); and two events into `app/Modules/Communication/Events` - `MessageSent`,
`NotificationSent` - because they name a Communication model and C1 says events go to their publisher.

**The move forced three things the plan did not list**, each of which the boundary suite caught:

1. `User`'s five reverse relations had 6 call sites, but two were *unused* (`conversations`,
   `sentMessages`) and the other four were internal accessors plus one controller. So the relations and
   both unread-count accessors are gone. The API still emits `unread_count` because Communication's
   `NotificationController` now asks the new `Contracts\UnreadNotificationCounter`
   (`Services\UnreadNotificationCountReader`) for it - the reader reproduces the old
   `belongsToMany` + `whereNull('read_at')` join exactly, so the number is unchanged.
2. The push-token listing endpoint used `$user->pushTokens()`. A controller may not import a model
   (`controllers_to_models` is 0), so the query moved into `PushNotificationService::activeTokensForUser()`
   - same rows, same `active()` scope, same JSON.
3. Console's `StaffChatController` constructed `new MessageSent(...)`. With the event now in Communication
   that is an illegal Console -> Communication *implementation* edge, so it goes through a new
   `Contracts\MessageBroadcaster` port (`Services\BroadcastingMessageBroadcaster`), whose parameter is
   deliberately untyped so the port cannot recreate the edge. This adds a fourth port on the existing
   Console -> Communication edge: recorded in `ModuleGraphTest::EDGES` with its reason, per that test's own
   instruction, and the table in its docblock was corrected 3 -> 4.

**Boundary evidence, before/after:** `controllers_to_models` 0 (unchanged), `kernel_use_of_module_contracts`
5 (unchanged - the `User` contract import I tried first was removed again rather than absorbed),
`kernel_files_may_not_name_module_implementation` 0, `CONSOLE_to_COMM` 0, `Console -> Communication` 3 -> 4
(documented), `DanglingImportTest` clean including `routes/channels.php`.

**A ratchet had to grow to stay honest.** `RV38LazyArmingMechanismTest` globbed `app/Models/*.php` and pinned
`>= 24` model files. After the move it saw 20 and failed - i.e. the sweep would have silently stopped
covering the moved cohort, the exact failure the trait prevents. It now globs `app/Models/*.php` **and**
`app/Modules/*/Models/*.php`, derives each FQCN from the file's own `namespace` line, and keeps the same
floor: 26 files. That is a stronger sweep, not a weaker assertion.

**Deploy notes: drain the queue before deploying.** Two moved classes use `SerializesModels` and can be
sitting in a serialized queue payload that names their old FQCN: `App\Events\MessageSent` and
`App\Events\NotificationSent`, now `App\Modules\Communication\Events\...`. A payload enqueued before the
deploy would fail to unserialize after it.

**Verification.** `php -l` on every changed file; whole-tree Pint clean (795 files). Scoped run over
Snapshots + Review + Admin + Notifications + Chat + AppFuture: **1052 tests, 5191 assertions, 3 failures**,
and the 3 are `L16DriverNoShowSettlementCharacterizationTest` - proved **pre-existing** by stashing the whole
change and re-running that file on HEAD, where it fails identically (3 of 4). `git status tests/Snapshots`
is empty: Phase C left the frozen corpus byte-identical, as required.

**Genuinely unverified:** the randomized ledger property and the five-order matrix (Phase E) do not cover
this module yet; and whether any third-party code serialized those two events outside the queue.

|---|---|---|

| tests | ~5 | everything else was the `$this->wallet` helper |

So the User `wallet` relation has roughly **25 real call sites**, 22 of them naming `Money`'s own model from
inside `Money` (`WalletController`, `PassengerWalletCharger`, `WalletRequestService`) where a module-local

### 271. Stage 2 Phase C1, module 2 (Money), part 1: the read door, built and pinned before anything moves

Module 2 cannot start with a file move. Everything Identity knows about a wallet arrives through
`$user->wallet` (`PassengerProfileQueryService::withWallet/withWalletOrFail`, `PassengerProfileController`
4 sites, `PassengerProfilePanelBuilder` 3 sites) and through a **direct model import** -
`PassengerProfilePanelBuilder` and `PassengerProfileQueryService` both do
`WalletTransaction::with([...])->where('wallet_id', ...)`. Once `Wallet`/`WalletTransaction` leave
`App\Models`, both are `Identity -> Money` implementation edges, which the boundary rules forbid and the
baselines may not absorb. So the port has to exist first.

**Added, inert** (nothing calls it yet, no response touched): `DTOs\WalletSummary` (read-only, property
names kept identical to the wallet columns so the existing response builders read the same names -
`PassengerWalletCharger::chargeSuccessResponse()` reads exactly `$wallet->balance`),
`Contracts\WalletDirectory` (`forUser()` and `summariesFor()`), `Services\WalletDirectoryReader`, and the
binding in `MoneyServiceProvider`.

**Why `summariesFor()` exists.** The naive port would be `forUser()` only, and every caller with a list
would loop it. The profile panel is exactly such a caller: it renders a balance next to rows that are
already batched, under a shrink-only query budget. So the contract carries a batched `byIds` form and the
test pins that it is **one query** for three users, and that `forUser()` is one query - not "some queries".
That is the objective's "no N+1" made executable rather than aspirational.

**Verification.** `php -l` on all four files; whole-tree Pint clean (799 files); new
`tests/Feature/Review/Stage2WalletDirectoryTest.php` **4 tests / 14 assertions**, including the two
query-count assertions; `tests/Feature/AppFuture` + `tests/Unit/Providers` + `tests/Feature/Wallet`
**132 tests / 557 assertions, OK** - the container change is inert today, as intended.

**What module 2 still needs** (next, in one commit so no violation ever exists in the tree): switch
Identity's 7 relation reads to `WalletDirectory` and its two `WalletTransaction` imports to a second port
(`WalletChargeHistory`, returning the same 12-key rows `formatWalletCharge` builds today, computed inside
Money so Identity stops formatting another module's model); drop `with('wallet')` from the two query methods
and `User::wallet()`; then move the four models. The budgets in the frozen corpus are the referee: if the
panel gains a query, the swap is wrong.

### 272. Stage 2 Phase C1, module 2 (Money), part 2a: the charge rows move into Money, and the snapshots prove nothing changed

**Moved**: the admin "wallet charges" row builder. It existed twice in Identity -

`PassengerProfilePanelBuilder::buildWalletCharges()` (last 20, for the profile bundle) - both querying
Money's `WalletTransaction` and both formatting through `PassengerProfilePanelBuilder::formatWalletCharge()`.

It now lives in Money as `Contracts\WalletChargeHistory` + `Services\WalletChargeHistoryReader`, with two
methods (`recentForWallet`, `paginateForWallet`) and the same query inside (same eager loads on

body moved verbatim rather than being rewritten, which is why `formatWalletCharge()` is deleted instead of
adapted: its output is now produced where the table is owned.

**Why this had to precede the model move.** Identity named `App\Models\WalletTransaction` directly in two
services. While that class lives in `App\Models` the boundary tests tolerate it; once it moves into the Money
namespace those two lines become `Identity -> Money` *implementation* edges, and the graph test says a new
port on an existing edge must be argued for rather than absorbed. So the port lands first, the edges stay
declared, and the model move becomes mechanical.

**Declared consequences.** `Identity -> Money` is now 2 ports, not 1 - recorded in
`ModuleGraphTest::EDGES` with the reason, and its docblock table row corrected (Money column 1 -> 2, after I
first bumped the Communication column by mistake and caught it). The controller's
`->map(fn ($tx) => $this->panels->formatWalletCharge($tx))` is gone because the collection already holds
formatted rows.

**Verification - the strong kind.** `tests/Feature/AppFuture` + the **whole** `tests/Feature/Snapshots`
suite: **242 tests, 2514 assertions, OK**, and `git status tests/Snapshots` is **empty**. That is the proof
that matters for this phase: the admin passenger profile JSON is byte-identical to the frozen corpus, and the
shrink-only query budgets still hold - the charge rows did not become an extra query or an N+1. Whole-tree
Pint clean, `php -l` on every touched file, autoload regenerated.

**Still open in module 2** (part 2b/2c): Identity's `createTransaction()` still writes Money's model (the
site of the parked double-injection defect), and 20 `$user->wallet` reads remain - 13 inside Money, 7 in
Identity. Those, `User::wallet()`, and the four model moves are the next commit; the write path needs a port
that does not change money semantics, which is why it is not being rushed in alongside a read swap.

### 273. Stage 2 Phase C1, module 2 (Money), part 2b: the cross-module write, moved without deciding the parked defect

Identity also **wrote** Money's table: `PassengerProfileQueryService::createTransaction()` called
`WalletTransaction::create($attributes)` and the admin charge flow consumed the returned row to link the
ledger leg. That is a cross-module write, illegal once the model moves.

Added `Contracts\WalletTransactionRecorder` (`record(array $attributes): mixed`) and
`Services\WalletTransactionRecorderService`, which is the previous call, unchanged. `createTransaction()`
now delegates and returns `mixed`; the row still flows into
`injectExternalCapital(..., $adminChargeTransaction)` exactly as before, so the ledger linkage B2 built is
untouched.

**What this port deliberately does NOT do.** The obvious "clean" move would be to have Money own the whole
admin-charge sequence - create the transaction *and* inject External Capital in one method - which would
also remove the duplicate injection. That is the parked defect (audit sec 264: one `+5000` credit with two
`-5000` external debits), and collapsing it changes money semantics, so it stays parked. The port does one
insert and nothing else, and its docblock says so, so a later reader cannot mistake the restraint for an
oversight. `mixed` rather than the model type is the same reasoning as the other ports: naming the type
recreates the import the port removes.

**Verification.** Snapshots + AppFuture + Admin + Review: **1027 tests, 5151 assertions**, the only failures
being the 3 pre-existing `L16DriverNoShow` ones; `git status tests/Snapshots` empty, so the admin charge
snapshot (which records the duplicated external debit) is byte-identical - the write path really is
unchanged. `Identity -> Money` is now 3 declared ports (was 1 before this phase), recorded with the reason in
`ModuleGraphTest::EDGES` and its docblock table row; AppFuture alone: 56 tests / 445 assertions OK.

**Remaining for module 2** (part 2c): 20 `$user->wallet` reads - 13 inside Money (WalletController 8,
PassengerWalletCharger 1, WalletRequestService 3, CashRideFeeService 1) and 7 in Identity - then
`User::wallet()`, `with('wallet')` in the two query methods, and the four model moves. The read migration has
a hard constraint worth stating before anyone starts it: **every replacement must issue exactly the same
number of queries**, because the budgets are frozen and `$user->wallet` is a cached relation - so a call must
be hoisted into a local, and a builder that needs the wallet must receive it from its caller rather than
looking it up again. A helper `Wallet::forUser()` returning one row per call is the right primitive.
